stories.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to solicit community input around AI data centers, publish construction plans and protect ratepayers.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
sources.text: OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI. The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws. "What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward." Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic , have outlined several similar commitments . On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI. AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio . OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then. "Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said. sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built. It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies. The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects. OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays. It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC. Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions. The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions. OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress. Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
sources.text: The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments. The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments. Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion , OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials. Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects. OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers ) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

stories.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
stories.summary: “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Clément Delangue said of the need for open source AI.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
sources.text: Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami. “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.” Hugging Face is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught. Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too. Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.” In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said. Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems. Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users. Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks , a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI. Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future. “We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.” Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: O risco da IA para a humanidade é ‘próximo de zero’, diz CEO da Hugging Face
sources.text: A inteligência artificial (IA) é perigosa em alguns aspectos, mas representa uma ameaça “próxima de zero” para a humanidade . A opinião é de Clément Delangue, CEO da Hugging Face. A plataforma é um repositório de códigos e modelos de IA, mais conhecida fora da indústria por ser até agora o alvo mais famoso de um agente rebelde da OpenAI. A opinião vai contra alguns pesquisadores do setor, que denunciam os possíveis riscos graves do crescimento acelerado da capacidade dessas ferramentas. Porém, o executivo crê que há “ muitos outros tópicos que podem destruir o mundo ” para além de um sistema automatizado. Delangue falou sobre o assunto durante um evento organizado pela Wired . No painel, o CEO defendeu ainda lutar pela criminalização de invasões cometidas por agentes de IA, mesmo os que estavam em ambientes de teste e “ saíram do controle ” dos responsáveis. “Ciberataques são ilegais, e considero fundamental garantir que ciberataques autônomos também sejam ilegais. Não queremos criar um cenário em que não haja responsabilização, em que ninguém responda” argumenta. Porém, a própria Hugging Face decidiu não processar ou denunciar a OpenAI após a tentativa de exploração de brechas. Atualmente de propriedade da Nvidia, a Hugging Face seguirá fomentando o mercado aberto de IA, para que modelos abertos e mais transparentes tenham cada vez mais espaço no mercado . Segundo Delangue, isso é essencial para evitar que a indústria da IA fique na mão de poucas empresas responsáveis — especialmente companhias que constroem modelos de ponta “ sob portas fechadas ” e em segredo, como é o caso da própria dona do ChatGPT. “É perfeitamente possível que acabemos em um mundo no qual apenas algumas empresas controlem a maior parte da IA. Existem tendências naturais muito fortes, já que elas acabam monopolizando talentos, poder computacional e capacidades”, alerta o executivo. A invasão da Hugging Face, segundo ele, é um exemplo disso: a companhia adotou um modelo aberto chinês, o GLM-5.2, para investigar e restringir os efeitos da invasão sofrida. A ideia da companhia é permitir que cada vez mais pessoas tenham acesso a modelos customizados de IA, o que ajudaria na formação de um “ futuro tecnológico mais democrático ”. Como a IA está ampliando os riscos de ataques cibernéticos no geral? stories.title: Sony vuelve a los ochenta con los MDR-3R, una versión modernizada de los auriculares para Walkman
stories.summary: La compañía japonesa ha reinterpretado los MDR-3 originales con un formato moderno y fiel al original, USB-C, micrófono integrado y un botón en el cable para llamadas.

sources.name: Computer Hoy
sources.title: Sony vuelve a los ochenta con los MDR-3R, una versión modernizada de los auriculares para Walkman
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. La compañía japonesa ha reinterpretado los MDR-3 originales con un formato moderno y fiel al original, USB-C, micrófono integrado y un botón en el cable para llamadas. Sony acaba de anunciar los MDR-3R, una reinterpretación de sus clásicos auriculares de los ochenta Walkman MDR-3, que vienen con cable USB-C, un micrófono integrado para llamadas, un mando a distancia en el propio cable para colgar el teléfono. Su precio es de 59 euros y, por el momento, no se ha concretado cuándo se pondrán a la venta en España, pero sí se ha avanzado que contarán con una versión adicional inspirada en Stranger Things. La empresa tecnológica nipona lanzó estos auriculares en 1979, junto con el Walkman, contribuyendo a crear una nueva manera de disfrutar de la música con total libertad y en cualquier lugar; una esencia que ahora quiere recuperar con un formato adaptado a los tiempos actuales. Los auriculares MDR-3R heredan el concepto de los originales, los MDR-3, de modo que están diseñados para que los usuarios puedan disfrutar de música y otros contenidos con total liberad en cualquier lugar, ya sea en interiores o al aire libre. De ese modo, conservan el diseño original , que refleja la tradición de la cultura audio portátil, al tiempo que incorporan características modernas de usabilidad. Entre ellas, la conectividad USB-C, sin interrupciones, un micrófono integrado para llamadas y un mano a distancia en el cable. Lo que sí que se mantienen son sus emblemáticas almohadillas azules y naranjas, gracias a lo cual los usuarios podrán mostrar su estado de ánimo o sus preferencias con ellas. Y, lo mejor de todo, es que el embalaje y el manual de instrucciones del modelo de los ochenta también se ha reproducido en esta ocasión. Los MDR-3R también recrean un diseño ligero y abierto, proporcionando una comodidad duradera incluso en sesiones de escucha prolongadas. Además, fomentan el plug-and-play para conectarlos rápidamente a los dispositivos compatibles y escuchar música, sin tener que cargarlos previamente o emparejarlos. También emplean los mismos transductores de sus predecesores, de 23 mm, para reproducir una calidad de sonido cercana a la original. No obstante, aunque se mantiene fiel a la firma sonora original, se han incorporado mejoras para adaptarse a las preferencias auditivas de la actualidad. Junto con la versión original, Sony ha anunciado el lanzamiento de una edición especial de estos auriculares , coincidiendo con la gran popularidad que ha tenido y aún conserva Stranger Things, una de las principales producciones de Netflix. Estos MDR-3 edición Stranger Things cuenta con detalles de diseño exclusivos, como es el caso del logotipo de la producción grabado en la diadema y un embalaje personalizado, que amplía la experiencia más allá de los propios auriculares.

sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: Sony revive los auriculares del Walkman de 1979 con los nuevos MDR-3R y se suma al regreso del audio con cable
sources.text: Hay algo curioso en el momento tecnológico que vivimos. Tenemos teléfonos capaces de hacer fotografías excelentes y, aun así, las cámaras digitales compactas vuelven a despertar interés ; llevamos años escuchando música por Bluetooth, pero los auriculares con cable también están recuperando atractivo . No son necesariamente pasos atrás. A veces buscamos una estética concreta, otras veces preferimos objetos sencillos o queremos prescindir de una batería más. En medio de tantas novedades, algunas ideas del pasado están encontrando una segunda vida, y el audio portátil es un buen ejemplo. Sony sabe muy bien lo que significa llevar la música a todas partes. En 1979 lanzó el Walkman TPS-L2 , aquel reproductor de casetes portátil que ayudó a transformar nuestros hábitos de escucha y que llegó acompañado de unos auriculares especialmente ligeros, los MDR-3L2. No eran un accesorio cualquiera, sino una parte esencial de una propuesta que permitía disfrutar de la música mientras caminábamos por la calle. Ahora, casi medio siglo después, la firma japonesa ha vuelto a mirar hacia sus orígenes para presentar los MDR-3R , unos nuevos auriculares inspirados en aquella primera generación. La recuperación no se limita al nombre. Basta con observar los MDR-3R para reconocer varios elementos de los auriculares originales : una diadema fina, la forma curvada de su estructura, las perforaciones laterales y hasta el logotipo. El fabricante mantiene una construcción abierta y ligera, con un peso de solo 38 gramos y una diadema ajustable. Hay también un detalle especialmente reconocible: las almohadillas intercambiables en azul y naranja , ambos juegos incluidos en la caja, que permiten cambiar su apariencia. El homenaje continúa en el embalaje y el manual de instrucciones, que también recuperan referencias visuales del modelo histórico. La apariencia mira al pasado, pero la forma de conectarlos responde a los dispositivos actuales. Los MDR-3R utilizan USB-C y prescinden del tradicional minijack de 3,5 milímetros , por lo que no pueden enchufarse directamente a una salida de audio analógica. El cable mide 1,2 metros e incorpora un micrófono y un mando para controlar la reproducción y gestionar las llamadas, sin baterías que recargar ni dispositivos que emparejar. Eso sí, necesitan un equipo compatible con USB Audio Class 1.0 , y Sony advierte de que algunas funciones pueden variar según el dispositivo, el sistema operativo o la aplicación. Curiosamente, tampoco recomienda utilizarlos con sus reproductores Walkman . En el apartado sonoro, los MDR-3R incorporan transductores de 23 milímetros , el mismo diámetro que los utilizados en los auriculares originales, y una configuración que, según el fabricante, busca recuperar su carácter acústico. La firma japonesa promete un sonido natural y equilibrado , especialmente en las voces, aunque reconoce haber introducido pequeños ajustes para adaptarlo a las preferencias actuales. Su construcción abierta, por otra parte, implica un aislamiento limitado frente al ruido exterior y permite que parte del sonido escape hacia fuera. Tampoco cuentan con cancelación activa de ruido, algo que conviene tener presente si pensamos utilizarlos en entornos concurridos. La mirada a los años ochenta también se extiende a una colaboración con Netflix. Sony ha anunciado una edición limitada de los MDR-3R inspirada en ' Stranger Things ', una serie cuya estética está estrechamente vinculada a aquella década. Esta versión tiene una diadema negra, incluye almohadillas intercambiables rojas y negras que recuerdan a los auriculares de Max y añade el logotipo de la producción grabado, además de un embalaje exclusivo inspirado en el Upside Down. En España, la versión convencional tiene un precio recomendado de 60 euros , frente a los 70 euros de esta edición especial. Sony sitúa la disponibilidad de ambos modelos en noviembre de 2026, sin concretar el día de lanzamiento en nuestro país. Las cifras ayudan a entender por qué el cable vuelve a encontrar su espacio. Según Circana , los ingresos por ventas de auriculares con cable aumentaron un 3% en Estados Unidos durante 2025, después de cinco años de descensos, y un 20% en las primeras seis semanas de 2026. Eso no significa que los modelos inalámbricos hayan perdido su posición dominante ni que sepamos cuánto pesará la nostalgia en las decisiones de compra. Lo interesante de la propuesta de Sony es que recupera un producto asociado a sus orígenes para ofrecerlo a consumidores que viven en un mundo tecnológico muy diferente al de 1979. La clave está en lo que representan: desconexión

sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
sources.text: Classified as ‘Critical,’ GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra on cyber-related benchmarks. Classified as ‘Critical,’ GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra on cyber-related benchmarks. OpenAI is launching GPT-6 Cyber , the latest version of its cybersecurity AI model, which it says is better at finding vulnerabilities and less likely to go rogue and hack other platforms in the process. OpenAI says that during testing, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds less than 1 percent of the time, down from around 5 percent with GPT-5.6 Cyber. The evaluation, called ExploitGym HoneyPot, is modeled after the Hugging Face Incident, in which OpenAI’s AI agents breached the open-source AI community to find answers to a problem they were tasked with solving. “With the 6 Cyber model, we were able to make huge improvements on this evaluation,” Fouad Matin, the head of OpenAI’s cyber preparedness and safety team, said during a press briefing. “It’s over 99 percent of the time doing what you ask.” But evaluation awareness , or when an AI system recognizes that it’s being tested and changes its behavior in response, remains a concern. “Evaluation awareness is super top of mind for us,” Matin said. “Often when we do see evaluation awareness, you’ll see it in the model’s chain of thought.” Matin added that OpenAI is trying to prioritize production-like evaluations, where the model is interacting with real codebases with a real objective to lessen the risk of awareness. Following a wave of AI cybersecurity incidents, OpenAI has raced to strengthen its safeguards and lock down its most powerful models. The company briefly paused training of its frontier AI models, and it now restricts their access to the internet . GPT-6 Cyber is classified as Critical in cybersecurity on OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework , which indicates that it “can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention.” GPT-5.6 Cyber was previously classified as High under the framework. GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s flagship Critical-level model , on most cyber-related tasks. In ExploitGym, an AI benchmark that measures whether an AI model can exploit vulnerabilities, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent, about 16 points higher than GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1 percent and a few points higher than GPT-6 Astra’s 42.4 percent score. The model helped find 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox, and it played a role in hardening OpenAI’s own infrastructure for training AI models, OpenAI says. Additionally, GPT-6 Cyber comes with stronger safeguards “to detect and disrupt misuse” while better adhering to user instructions. OpenAI says it’s using new checks to block “high-risk activity,” including attacks on critical infrastructure like power plants and water treatment facilities. GPT-6 Cyber is rolling out to select members of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red program, which is available to companies and organizations using its models for “authorized defensive cybersecurity work.” It’s expanding GPT-6 Cyber to all Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
sources.text: Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system. Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models. “I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!” He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models. “I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.” OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser. “Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement. OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits. Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems. The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails . Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers. It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.” But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics. If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required. sources.title: Muse has a voice mode now
sources.text: Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you. Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you. Meta now lets you have voice conversations with your Muse AI agent in real time, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced today . The feature has been rolled out to me, and I gave it a spin on the iOS app while writing this article. As you chat with your Muse agent, the avatar at the top of your conversation animates in time with the words that it’s saying. You can also change the tone of the voice by just asking your agent about what you want and letting it decide or by browsing through a bunch of options in the avatar settings. In my brief tests, my Muse agent responds quickly over voice, though it occasionally pauses while it’s looking up information or checking something for me (like it would with a text chat query). It also animates what it’s saying well, though for my particular avatar, it’s been a little uncanny. I set my Muse agent’s avatar to look like Mark Zuckerberg as a constant reminder that I’m chatting with a Meta service (I refuse to be charmed by a Jolly! ), and seeing the digital Zuckerberg facsimile actually talk with me is quite weird. I also can’t get my Muse agent’s voice to sound exactly like Mark Zuckerberg. Muse’s voice mode and expressive avatars are rolling out now in the US for the app, Meta says . They’re coming “soon” for Meta’s AI glasses and will also be available for its forthcoming Muse Charm gadget , which is supposed to ship this year.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
sources.text: Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday. First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user. While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character. The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it. As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.) The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!) The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them. Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device. stories.title: Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
stories.summary: Airbnb says its upcoming AI agent will help travelers plan trips, compare options, manage bookings, and get assistance throughout their stay.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
sources.text: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year. Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter released today . “Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge. Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work: We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb. Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said before that the company plans to launch an agent in 2027, telling the Skift Global Forum that it would have an interface that’s “much richer than a chatbot.” In its shareholder letter, Airbnb also said that AI is “the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb” and has changed how it develops products and operates.
